chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl from al-Abbas ibn Amir from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: Is it permissible for anyone to take back a charity (sadaqah) or a gift (hibah)? He said: 'As for what is given as charity for the sake of Allah, it is not taken back. And as for the gift (hibah) and the grant (nihlah), one may take it back whether one has taken possession of it or not, even if it was given to a relative.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is understood to apply when the recipient is a mature, fully competent adult, because if he were a child, it would not be permissible for him to take it back. Or we may understand it to apply to those relatives other than children. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.نِحْلَة: Grant or endowment (a type of gift)

ai.seo_question: Can a giver take back a gift or charity in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a fundamental juristic distinction where *sadaqah* (charity) becomes irrevocable once given for Allah's sake, while *hibah* (gift) remains revocable by the donor even before physical possession (*qabd*), extending to relatives. The commentary by Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that this revocability presupposes a mature, competent recipient, as minors lack the legal capacity to effectuate such a return. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the donor's continued ownership rights in gifts until full transfer, contrasting with the more permanent nature of charitable endowments.
